extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers learning algebraic geometry (schemes/morphisms)
extracted.subtask_description: Define and characterize many useful classes of morphisms of schemes (reasonable classes, open embeddings, quasicompact/quasiseparated, affine, finite, integral) and present key theorems (Lying Over, Going-Up, Nakayama) and examples/exercises illustrating these notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable class of morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Any class of morphisms satisfying three basic properties: (i) preserved by composition; (ii) preserved by base change (pullback/fibered product); (iii) local on the target (stable under restriction to opens and can be checked on an open cover of the target).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: (iv) preserved by products and (v) the Cancellation Theorem. When learning a new class of morphisms, immediately check (i)–(iii); if one fails, be cautious and consider refining the definition. Examples to test: injections, surjections, open embeddings, closed embeddings in topological spaces; many scheme-classes satisfy these properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open embedding (open immersion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is an open embedding (open immersion) if it factors as an isomorphism onto an open subscheme (i.e., π factors as X ≅ (U, O_Y|U) ↪ Y where U ⊂ Y is open).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate facts: isomorphisms are open embeddings; notation often uses '↪' to indicate open embedding. Distinguish between 'open embedding' (a bijection onto an open subset as a morphism) and 'open subscheme' (an actual subset). Exercises: verify open embeddings satisfy the 'reasonable' properties; show fibered products with open embeddings exist and open embeddings are monomorphisms. Hints: check behavior on distinguished opens, determinants not vanishing in glueing arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local on the source/target and affine-local
rubrics_metrics.description: For a property P of morphisms: 'local on the target' means P can be checked after restricting to an open cover of the target; 'local on the source' means P can be checked on an open cover of the source. 'Affine-local' means checking suffices on affine open covers (useful because criteria on affines are simpler).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Affine Communication Lemma (referenced) to pass between affine-local checks and global conclusions. The text emphasizes verifying afﬁne-locality for properties like affineness, finiteness, integrality, quasicompactness and quasiseparatedness. Examples/exercises: show affineness and finiteness are affine-local on the target; quasicompactness/quasiseparatedness are affine-local on the target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasicompact morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is quasicompact if for every open affine U ⊂ Y, the preimage π^{-1}(U) is quasicompact (equivalently, preimage of any quasi-compact open is quasi-compact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quasicompactness because finiteness conditions simplify arguments (e.g., induction). Exercises: composition of quasicompact morphisms is quasicompact; morphisms from Noetherian schemes are quasicompact. Quasicompactness is afﬁne-local on the target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasiseparated morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is quasiseparated if for every affine open U ⊂ Y, the scheme π^{-1}(U) is quasiseparated (equivalently preimage of any quasi-compact open is quasiseparated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quasiseparatedness is often paired with quasicompactness (abbreviated 'qcqs'); many natural morphisms (locally Noetherian sources, affine, separated) are quasiseparated. Note: composition of quasiseparated morphisms is true but not obvious; will be clearer after diagonal/quasicompact diagonal characterization (11.2.4). Quasiseparatedness is afﬁne-local on the target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is affine if for every affine open U = Spec B ⊂ Y, the preimage π^{-1}(U) is an affine scheme (Spec A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affineness is afﬁne-local on the target (proved via the Affine Communication Lemma and Qcqs Lemma). Immediate facts: composition of affine morphisms is affine; affine morphisms are quasicompact and quasiseparated. Proof guidance sketches how to reconstruct X as Spec Γ(X, O_X) using covers and the Qcqs Lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is finite if for every affine open Spec B ⊂ Y, π^{-1}(Spec B) = Spec A with A a finite (i.e., finitely generated as a B-module) B-algebra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finite morphisms are affine by definition. Key properties and examples: finite ⇒ integral; finite morphisms are projective (exercise), have finite fibers, and are closed maps (images of closed sets are closed). Examples: branched covers Spec k[t] → Spec k[u] given by u = p(t); closed embeddings Spec A/I → Spec A; normalization maps like Spec k[t] → nodal cubic. Exercises show finiteness is afﬁne-local on the target; composition of finite morphisms is finite. Anti-patterns: morphisms with finite fibers that are not finite (e.g., open embedding A^2 \{0} → A^2 is affine with finite fibers but not finite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is integral if it is affine and for every affine open Spec B ⊂ Y with π^{-1}(Spec B) = Spec A, the induced ring map B → A is integral (every element of A satisfies a monic polynomial with coefficients in B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integral is an afﬁne-local condition and is closed under composition. Finite ⇒ integral (Corollary 8.2.2), but integral need not imply finite (example: Q ⊂ Q as map illustrating non-finiteness). Integral morphisms give rise to useful algebraic theorems (Lying Over, Going-Up).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lying Over Theorem (for integral extensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ : B → A is an integral extension, then for any prime ideal q ⊂ B there exists a prime p ⊂ A with p ∩ B = q (i.e., primes upstairs lie over primes downstairs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric translation: Spec A → Spec B is surjective when A is integral over B. Proof approach: localize at q to reduce to local case and then pick a maximal ideal of A and use that B/(p∩B) is a field (exercise). Illustrative figure and exercises accompany the statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Going-Up Theorem (for integral extensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ : B → A is integral, chains of primes in B can be lifted/extended to chains of primes in A: given q1 ⊂ ... ⊂ qn in B and p1 ⊂ ... ⊂ pm in A with pi lying over qi (and m < n), then the chain upstairs can be extended to length n preserving the lying-over property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an important exercise (8.2.F) with hints: reduce to small cases and use Lying Over. The text suggests drawing a picture akin to Figure 8.1 to understand the theorem. (Going-Down results exist under different hypotheses and are discussed later.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Nakayama's Lemma (several versions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several related statements about finitely generated modules over rings with ideals in the Jacobson radical: Version 1 — if M is finitely generated over A and M = I M for I an ideal, then there exists a ∈ 1 + I with aM = 0 (equivalently some element ≡ 1 mod I annihilates M). Version 2 — if I is contained in all maximal ideals and M = I M then M = 0. Version 4 — over a local ring (A, m), generators of M/mM lift to generators of M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the adjugate/determinant trick from Lemma 8.2.1. Consequences: lifting generators, applications to generating maximal ideals from m/m^2, and several exercises generalizing the lemma. Geometric interpretations and exercises follow (e.g., Exercise 14.3.E).

rubrics_metrics.name: General guidance: check properties on affine covers and use exercises/examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Many properties of morphisms (quasicompact, quasiseparated, affine, finite, integral, etc.) are afﬁne-local on the target and should be checked on affine open covers; exercises demonstrate typical verifications and counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Afﬁne Communication Lemma and Qcqs Lemma to pass between local affine checks and global conclusions. The text repeatedly provides exercises that show how to reduce global statements to affine computations and gives counterexamples (e.g., non-quasicompact embeddings) to illustrate pitfalls.
